The Bronze Age. Roughly from thirty-three hundred to twelve hundred BCE, this prehistoric and ancient period was defined by the widespread use of bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, for tools, weapons, and ornaments. The Bronze Age witnessed the rise of complex civilizations, long-distance trade networks, writing systems, and sophisticated social hierarchies, marking a leap from the Stone Age toward organized urban societies.

Bronze, being harder and more durable than copper or tin alone, revolutionized tool-making and warfare. Bronze weapons and armor gave wielders decisive advantages, reshaping military organization and social power. The Bronze Age emerged at different times globally, roughly thirty-three hundred BCE in Mesopotamia and the Aegean, later in Europe and China. The Shang Dynasty in ancient China was one of the world's first literate Bronze Age civilizations.

Major Bronze Age civilizations included the Minoans of Crete, the Mycenaeans of Greece, the Hittites of Anatolia, the Egyptian Middle Kingdom, and the Indus Valley Civilization, each creating distinct cultures yet linked by trade. Bronze Age trade networks connected the Mediterranean, Anatolia, Mesopotamia, Egypt, and beyond as merchants exchanged tin from Afghanistan, copper from Cyprus, cedar from Lebanon, and luxury goods including ivory and lapis lazuli.

Writing emerged during the Bronze Age in multiple regions. Cuneiform appeared in Mesopotamia, hieroglyphics in Egypt, Linear A and B in the Aegean, and oracle bone script in China, each adapted to recording administrative, religious, and economic information. The Bronze Age Collapse around twelve hundred BCE saw the abrupt fall of major civilizations including Mycenaean Greece, the Hittite empire, and declining Egyptian New Kingdom power due to invasions, climate change, and economic disruption, fragmenting the interconnected Bronze Age world.

The transition to the Iron Age occurred as iron-working technology spread, making iron tools and weapons more available and affordable than bronze, eventually replacing bronze as the primary metal.
